title: git: snapshots, branches and undo
summary: What a commit and a branch are, how to settle a merge conflict, put work aside, and undo a change before or after a commit.

scheme: staging: what goes in the next snapshot
history: a snapshot, saved for good
text: A commit is a snapshot of your project, with a message saying why.
- git add picks what goes in; git commit saves it.
- git status tells you what is changed, staged, or untracked (new to git).
- git diff --staged shows exactly what the commit will change: read it first.
The history is a chain: each commit points to the one before.
- git log --oneline shows it, newest first.
- A branch is only a label on a commit. main (master in some repositories) is a branch like any other.
- HEAD is where you are: it points to your branch.
git switch -c login-fix makes a new label and moves you to it.
- New commits go on your branch; main doesn't move.
- When it works, git switch main, then git merge login-fix brings it in.

scheme: Dessert: chocolate cake   the other branch
text: When two branches change the same line, git merge can't choose: it stops and writes both sides into the file.
- Above ======= is your side (HEAD), below it the other branch's.
- Edit the file so it reads the way you want, and delete the three marker lines.
- git add marks it as settled; git commit finishes the merge.
- Lost? git merge --abort puts everything back as it was before the merge.

scheme: clean tree: switch, fix, commit, come back
│  git stash pop   take it back
text: An urgent fix comes in while your work is half done, and it isn't ready to commit.
- git stash puts your changes aside and leaves a clean tree.
- git stash list shows what is aside; back on your branch, git stash pop brings the last one back.
- Files git doesn't track yet stay where they are: git stash -u takes them too.

scheme: ▼  unstages: your file keeps the change
▼  drops what you didn't git add
text: Before a commit, git restore undoes things.
- git restore file throws away the changes you haven't git add-ed yet, for good: read the name twice.
- git restore --staged file only unstages it: the change stays, it just won't go in the next commit.
- git status reminds you of both commands.

scheme: a1 ◀─ b2 ◀─ c3 ◀─ main        b2 is the bad one
a1 ◀─ b2 ◀─ c3 ◀─ d4 ◀─ main  d4 undoes b2
text: A commit others already pulled stays in the history. git revert makes a new commit that does the opposite.
- The history only grows: everyone pulls again, and nothing breaks. If a later commit changed the same lines, revert stops on a conflict: settle it like a merge, git add, then git revert --continue.
- git reset moves the branch back: the commits after it leave the branch, their changes stay in your files.
- git reset --hard throws those changes away too, with your uncommitted work: keep reset for commits that never left your machine.
